title: Tools & Resources
text:
Methods I use, and why
A short, opinionated list — the methods that come up most often in my work and the problem each one actually solves.







Method
The problem it solves




Linear mixed-effects models
Repeated nights within a person are not independent observations


Mundlak within/between decomposition
Separates “hot nights change what people do” from “heat changes what their body does”


Segmented / piecewise regression with AIC knot search
Finds where an exposure–response relationship actually bends, rather than assuming it is a straight line


Restricted cubic splines
Lets the shape of a dose–response curve be estimated, not imposed


Cluster-robust standard errors and cluster bootstrap
Honest uncertainty when observations come in groups


PRISMA 2020 / PROSPERO registration
Makes a review’s decisions checkable, and its scope fixed before the results are known

title: Tools & Resources
text:
Software
heatsviz — contributor to the internal visualisation package used across Project HEATS, providing a consistent figure grammar and export presets for manuscripts and slides in both R and Python.
Reproducible reporting — most of my analysis pipelines are Python (statsmodels, pandas, seaborn, python-docx, PyMuPDF) with R for figures (tidyverse, ggplot2), version controlled in Git and written up in Quarto.

If a tool here is useful to you, please use it — attribution is welcome but not required. If something is broken or wrong, tell me and I will fix it.

title: Working with me
text: The quickest way to reach me is mrenard@nus.edu.sg. This page sets out what I can usefully help with, so you can tell in about a minute whether it is worth an email.

title: Working with me
text:
Research collaboration
I am most useful to a project that needs one of the following:

Statistical analysis of longitudinal or clustered data — repeated measures, wearable and sensor streams, field studies where the same people are observed many times. Mixed-effects modelling, within/between decomposition, non-linear threshold estimation.
Exposure–response and threshold work — where the question is not “is there an effect” but “at what point, and for whom”.
Evidence synthesis done properly — protocol development, PROSPERO registration, search strategy, risk of bias, and synthesis that survives peer review. I have registered four reviews and act as guarantor on one.
Turning findings into guidance — translating modelled results into thresholds and advisory language that an agency can actually adopt.

I work across environmental physiology, sleep, public health and nutritional science, and I am comfortable being the quantitative member of a team whose subject expertise is elsewhere.

title: Working with me
text:
Early career researchers
Much of my week is spent supporting teams of early career researchers — on analysis planning, coding practice, interpretation and scientific writing — across projects on dormitory heat and sleep, nighttime heat thresholds, cooling interventions and heat vulnerability index development.
If you are working in heat, sleep or environmental physiology and are stuck on a methods or analysis question, I am happy to talk. When you write, it helps enormously if you include the question that interests you and why, rather than a general expression of interest.
I also support early career researchers more broadly through the NUS Medicine Postdoctoral Association, where I lead the Education Subcommittee, and through the Early Career Researchers Office.

title: Working with me
text:
Media and speaking
My work on indoor heat and sleep has been covered in The Straits Times and Lianhe Zaobao. I am glad to speak to journalists about heat, sleep and health in tropical climates, and to give talks or workshops — particularly on statistical methods for researchers who did not train as statisticians.

A note on what I will not be much use for. I am not a clinician and cannot advise on individual health. I do not take on analysis-only work with no scientific involvement. And if a request needs an answer this week, please say so in the first line — my calendar is usually the constraint, not my interest.

title: Michèle Renard
text:
Research Fellow · Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore

I am an environmental physiologist and quantitative researcher working on how heat shapes sleep, physiological strain and health in real-world populations.

Most of my work sits where field measurement meets statistical modelling: large longitudinal wearable and sensor datasets, randomised cooling interventions in homes and dormitories, and systematic reviews that feed directly into national heat-health policy. I lead the statistical analysis for two national research programmes — Project HEATS and Cooling Singapore 2.0 — and work alongside teams of early career researchers across both.

title: Research
text:
My research asks a deceptively simple question: how much heat is too much, and for whom? Answering it means measuring people where they actually live and sleep, modelling exposure–response relationships that are rarely linear, and then turning those relationships into thresholds that a public health agency can act on.
Three strands run through the work — field measurement, statistical modelling, and evidence synthesis — and most projects use all three.

title: Research
section: Project HEATS — Heat Exposure, Activity and Sleep
text:
Project HEATS — Heat Exposure, Activity and Sleep
Analytical lead · NRF CREATE programme · 2025–present
Project HEATS characterises the indoor thermal environment of Singapore homes and dormitories and links it to objectively measured sleep. I lead the statistical analysis and manuscript development for the heat exposure workstream.
Design. Wearable and in-home monitoring across three field waves (Jun 2025 – Jul 2026): bedroom temperature, humidity, CO₂ and particulates alongside actigraphy-derived sleep outcomes. The primary analysis covers 122 participants and 10,303 person-nights.
Methods. Linear mixed-effects models with Mundlak within/between decomposition, which lets us separate what a person does in response to a hot night (behavioural adaptation) from what heat does to them (physiological strain) — a distinction that a single pooled coefficient hides. Non-linear threshold work uses piecewise and segmented models with AIC-based knot search and restricted cubic splines, comparing dry-bulb temperature against composite indices (wet-bulb temperature, Heat Index) as predictors of sleep disruption.
Outputs. A protocol paper under review at BMC Public Health; the primary sleep-continuity analysis in preparation; three oral presentations at Indoor Air 2026; a 30-night field trial of a dynamic “down-rise” bedroom cooling profile.

Findings from this programme were covered nationally in The Straits Times and Lianhe Zaobao in June 2026, and cited by the Chairman of the National Research Foundation Singapore.

title: Research
text:
Exertional Heat Vulnerability Index (eHVI)
Evidence-synthesis lead · protocol lead and guarantor · NRF & NEA, CISR-2024-2R-04
A Climate Impact Science Research programme building a heat vulnerability index for Singapore. I lead the evidence-synthesis workstream: I developed the systematic review protocol underpinning the index — search strategy, extraction framework and synthesis approach — and serve as guarantor of the review. I also chair the bi-weekly technical review and act as quality gate for the report blocks delivered to the funder.
Registered as PROSPERO CRD420261289729.

title: Research
text:
Cooling Singapore 2.0
Analytical lead, physiological workstream · NRF
Controlled laboratory heat-exposure studies across population groups who are usually treated as a single “general public” in advisory design: children, heat-unacclimatised adults and older adults. I model the physiological and perceptual responses and translate them into policy-relevant insight for tailoring national heat-health advisories — the point being that one threshold for everyone protects nobody particularly well.

title: Research
text:
Behaviour, nutrition and health
My doctoral and postdoctoral work addressed a parallel question in a different domain: what determines what people actually eat, and which of those determinants can be moved?

Team sport athletes (PhD, TUS Athlone) — dietary intake against sports nutrition guidelines, nutrition knowledge, and cooking and food skills, using a mixed-methods design to identify modifiable behavioural targets.
UK households in the cost-of-living crisis (King’s College London) — cooking and food behaviours, food insecurity, diet quality and mental wellbeing, combining hierarchical regression on large survey datasets with thematic analysis of focus group and open-text data.

The methodological thread — behaviour is a modifiable exposure, and you have to measure it well before you can change it — is the same one that runs through the heat work.
